youtube.title: The nut that rises | Reality Rulebook Season 2 · Episode 3
youtube.caption:
Where will the nut end up? Starting underneath everything.

Shake a jar of mixed nuts, or a box of cereal, and the biggest pieces often rise to the top. It's called the Brazil nut effect. It happens even when the big pieces are heavier, so it isn't just buoyancy. Small grains tumble into the gaps under the big one, grains can flow in a loop up the walls and down the middle, and in some jars the big ones sink instead.

Season 2 · Episode 3.

Sources
1. Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science', arXiv:2201.12128 (full text read by the builder, 9 Nov 2026): https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12128
2. Rosato, Strandburg, Prinz, Swendsen, 'Why the Brazil nuts are on top: size segregation of particulate matter by shaking', Phys. Rev. Lett. 58, 1038 (1987) (search excerpt only, not opened): https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.1038
3. Deegan et al., 'Capillary flow as the cause of ring stains from dried liquid drops', Nature 389, 827 (1997) (for the next episode's teaser; search excerpt only, not opened): https://doi.org/10.1038/39827

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. The jar is a 3-D drawing of our own 2-D computer simulation (a simple model, not a measurement: it passes about 15 cm after about ten seconds of simulated shaking); the jar where a lighter big ball sinks is an illustration, not a simulation.
